question: Regardless of who loaded and secured the cargo, which of the following is one of the driver's stated responsibilities?
choice_a: Filing insurance claims for the shipper
choice_b: Determining the retail value of the cargo
choice_c: Recognizing overloads and poorly balanced weight
explanation: The manual lists inspecting cargo, recognizing overloads and poor weight balance, knowing cargo is secured and doesn't obscure your view, and knowing cargo doesn't restrict access to emergency equipment as driver responsibilities.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: After beginning a trip, within how many miles should you inspect the cargo and its securing devices again?
explanation: The manual states cargo and its securing devices must be inspected again within the first 50 miles after beginning a trip.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

topic: Cargo re-check interval during a trip
question: Besides after every break you take, the manual says you must re-check cargo:
explanation: The manual specifies re-checking cargo after you have driven for 3 hours or 150 miles, in addition to after every break.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: Gross Vehicle Weight Rating (GVWR) is defined in the manual as:
choice_a: The maximum safe weight a tire can carry
choice_b: The manufacturer's rating for a suspension system
choice_c: The value specified by the manufacturer as the loaded weight of a single vehicle
choice_d: The weight transmitted to the ground by one axle
explanation: GVWR is the value specified by the manufacturer as the loaded weight of a single vehicle.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: Which of the following matches the manual's definition of "axle weight"?
choice_a: The maximum weight a tire can carry at a specified pressure
choice_b: The weight transmitted to the ground by one axle or one set of axles
choice_c: The value specified by the manufacturer as loaded weight of a vehicle
choice_d: The rated maximum weight a coupling device can pull or carry
explanation: The manual defines axle weight as the weight transmitted to the ground by one axle or one set of axles.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: The bridge formula referenced in the manual, used to set maximum axle weights, permits:
choice_a: The same axle weight regardless of spacing
choice_b: More maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together
choice_c: Unlimited axle weight regardless of axle spacing
choice_d: Less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together
explanation: The manual explains that a bridge formula permits less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together, to prevent overloading bridges and roadways.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1 to 3-2

question: Per the manual, what effect can overloading a truck have?
choice_a: Increased stopping distance, with brakes that can fail when forced to work too hard
explanation: The manual states that overloading increases stopping distance and that brakes can fail when forced to work too hard.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: To reduce the chance of tipping over from a high center of gravity, the manual advises you to:
choice_a: Put the heaviest parts of the cargo under the lightest parts
choice_b: Distribute weight evenly without regard to height
choice_c: Load all cargo at the rear of the vehicle
choice_d: Put the heaviest parts of the cargo on top
explanation: The manual advises distributing cargo so it is as low as possible, putting the heaviest parts of the cargo under the lightest parts.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

topic: Weight balance on the steering axle
question: According to the manual, what problem can too much weight on the steering axle cause?
choice_a: Poor traction on the drive wheels
choice_d: Hard steering, and damage to the steering axle and tires
explanation: The manual states too much weight on the steering axle can cause hard steering and can damage the steering axle and tires.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: Federal regulations cited in the manual require the aggregate working load limit of a cargo securement system to be at least:
choice_a: Equal to the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_b: Twice the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_c: One-quarter the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_d: One-half times the weight of the article or group of articles
explanation: The manual states the aggregate working load limit of any securement system must be at least one-half times the weight of the article or group of articles.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: The manual says cargo should have at least one tie-down for every ten feet of cargo, with a minimum of how many tie-downs no matter how small the cargo is?
explanation: The manual states cargo should have at least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, and no matter how small the cargo, it should have at least two tie-downs.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: What is the purpose of a front-end header board ("headache rack"), per the manual?
choice_a: To display the vehicle's weight rating
choice_c: To secure tarps over the load
choice_d: To protect the driver from the cargo in a crash or emergency stop
explanation: The manual states front-end header boards protect the driver from the cargo in case of a crash or emergency stop, and should block the forward movement of cargo.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: The manual gives two basic reasons for covering cargo. What are they?
choice_a: To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather
choice_b: To reduce noise and increase visibility
choice_c: To reduce wind resistance and improve fuel economy
choice_d: To prevent theft and improve the vehicle's appearance
explanation: The manual lists the two basic reasons for covering cargo as protecting people from spilled cargo and protecting the cargo from weather.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: Since you cannot inspect a sealed load directly, what must you still check, per the manual?
choice_c: That you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits
explanation: The manual states you cannot inspect sealed loads, but you should check that you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: According to the manual, why does livestock require special driving care even when a trailer has less than a full load?
choice_b: Livestock always exceeds legal weight limits
choice_c: Livestock can move around and, even when bunched with false bulkheads, can lean on curves and shift the center of gravity
choice_d: Livestock must be tied down individually like sealed cargo
explanation: The manual explains livestock can move around causing unsafe handling; with less than a full load, false bulkheads are used to bunch livestock, but even then livestock can lean on curves, shifting the center of gravity and making rollover more likely.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3
